title: Kenny Bednarek, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden win 200m titles to complete American sprint sweep
content:
BUDAPEST, Hungary — American duo Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and Kenny Bednarek completed a sprint double at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships, winning their 200m races in world-leading times after claiming the 100m titles on Saturday night.

Jefferson-Wooden, who won three sprint golds at the world championships last September, ran 21.47s to give her the victory by three tenths over Olympic champion Gabby Thomas (21.77s, second). It also rockets her from ninth to third on the all-time list — only Shericka Jackson of Jamaica (21.41s) and world-record holder Florence Griffith-Joyner (21.34s) have ever run quicker.

“I’m speechless, honestly. I knew I wanted to PB so I was thinking 21.6-low or 21.5s. I skipped right over (that) and went to 21.4s,” Jefferson-Wooden said in the mixed zone. “The biggest thing my coach always tells me is to drive to 40m — once it was time to go into the curve, I just wanted to race, to let it come to me, not to rush any phase.”

Coming off the bend, Jefferson-Wooden led by nine hundredths and she showed better endurance than anyone else, extending her lead over Thomas, an athlete known for having top-end speed.

Bednarek clocked 19.52s to win, the fastest time of 2026 and an improvement to his personal best of five hundredths. He’s now the seventh-fastest man ever and, like Jefferson-Wooden, beat the Olympic gold medallist as Botswana’s Letsile Tebogo was more than two tenths off him in second place.

“We’ve got a bunch of dogs in our group,” Bednarek said in the mixed zone of Star Athletics. “I feel like this was a big year and a big step in my career, all year I’ve been having a good bend, it was more about finishing the tail end of the race. It was great execution.”

“The 200m is my thing, once I cracked the code in the 100m, I don’t want to say it released me, but I didn’t have pressure on myself,” Bednarek added, with a perfect record from six 200m races this year.

With $150,000 awarded to each individual winner at these championships, Bednarek and Jefferson-Wooden will take home $300,000 — they won their 100m finals in 9.85s and 10.62s respectively.

The performances this weekend are especially significant for Bednarek. He has proved himself a winner on the global stage, ending his streak of four silver medals and capitalising on the absence of fellow American Noah Lyles, the four-time 200m world champion who ended his season early through injury.

Elsewhere in Budapest, Josh Kerr won the men’s 1500m in 3:29.35s, dropping a 52.57s last lap. He held his nerve and spent most of the race deeper in the field rather than running from the front.

Robert Farken of Germany led for the first two laps, with modest splits of 57.09s at 400m and 1:55.29s at 800m resulting in athletes bunching up behind him. American Yared Nuguse made the decisive move with 600m to go, which strung the field out, and Kerr moved up to third as they hit the bell. The Briton waited until the back straight of the final lap to overtake Nuguse, and once he took the lead he never relinquished it.

Kerr was the quickest in the final 200m, closing that in 26.02s and finishing half a second clear of Australia’s Cameron Myers, while U.S trio Hobbs Kessler, Cole Hocker and Nuguse finished third, fourth and fifth. It’s a repeat of the Commonwealth Games mile final, where Kerr won gold on home soil in Glasgow ahead of Myers.

Back in March, Kerr became world indoor 3000m champion for the second time, and then spent months preparing for a takedown of Hicham El Guerrouj’s mile world record. He achieved that at the London Diamond League, running 3:42.66s to chop 0.47s off a mark that had stood since 1999.

Alison dos Santos, who broke the 400m hurdles world record in Zurich last month, produced another sub-46 performance to beat long-standing rivals Rai Benjamin (46.40s, second) and Karsten Warholm (46.78s, third). Dos Santos, running from lane seven, ran 45.98s, the third-fastest performance ever and just 0.18s off the record. He benefited, like in Zurich, from having the fast-starting Warholm in the lane outside, while Benjamin closed the gap to the Brazilian athlete on the second bend, only to fatigue on the home straight.

It’s the second time at these championships that Benjamin has finished runner-up, meaning he takes home a combined $150,000, following his 44.15s run over the 400m flat.

“It couldn’t have gone any better, well I could have won, that would have been perfect, but I clipped hurdle eight with my trail leg and was like, ‘yeah, it’s over,’” Benjamin said in the mixed zone. “You can’t make mistakes out there with these guys, they’ll punish you.” He added that he was proud of himself for doubling — racing four times over three days — and that “no one else could have come out here and done that”.

Benjamin, though, played down the idea of doubling up at next year’s World Championships in Beijing, or at a home Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028. “It’s not that I can’t, but it would be very idiotic,” he said, noting the demanding racing schedule at U.S. championship, where, ahead of the next Games, he would need a top three finish to make the team in both events.

Fellow American 400m hurdler Dalilah Muhammad announced her retirement following her 53.11s run for fourth. Muhammad, 36, won Olympic gold at the 2016 Games and was world champion three years later, in addition to being part of multiple gold-medal winning 4x400m relay teams.

Across more than a decade on the international stage, she twice broke the world record, with her 52.20s clocking in July 2019 bettering a mark that had stood for 16 years. “There have been so many emotions happening today,” she said in the mixed zone. “It never really hits you until you finish your career and see what you have accomplished.”

Sri Lankan thrower Rumesh Parthirage capped an outstanding season by throwing 91.09m with his final effort to win the men’s javelin, beating Grenada’s Anderson Peters by nearly five metres (86.18m). Parthirage, only 23, has won all but one of his 12 competitions this year including Commonwealth and Diamond League titles.

The U.S. won the mixed 4x400m relay on Sunday, adding to their victory in the 4x100m event on Friday, while Charlotte Henrich produced a storming 49.53s anchor leg to take Great Britain from fourth to second, overtaking the Netherlands (third) and Belgium (fourth).
